author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell reacts to a protest in Britain and argues that religious and cultural division is distracting people from what he sees as a much bigger issue: institutions gaining more control while ordinary people remain divided against one another.

He says there is no point in “phony tribalism” between different faiths and instead urges people to focus on the systems and institutions accumulating power at a global level.

The conversation then turns to surveillance, facial-recognition technology and concerns about people being arrested over social media posts, before Russell notes that the protester in the clip was ultimately arrested.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell reflects on the way the media treats high-profile women, using Caroline Flack and Princess Diana as examples of what he sees as a much deeper pattern than simply irresponsible reporting. He references the documentary The Corporation, which argues that if a corporation were treated like a person, its behavior could resemble that of a psychopath, and applies that idea to media institutions acting as a collective, even when individual journalists may believe they are simply doing their jobs.

The most disturbing part of his argument is the speed with which that same media machine can switch roles. Someone can be relentlessly scrutinized, mocked and torn apart while they are alive, only for the tone to change completely the moment they die, with grief, sympathy and nostalgia becoming the next thing to sell.

A sharp and uncomfortable reflection on media culture, public spectacle, and the way famous women can be turned into content at every stage of their lives.
